newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Australia hints at apology to "stolen" Aborigines.
newsitem.headline: Australia hints at apology to "stolen" Aborigines.

text.p: A senior Australian minister on Sunday signalled that Canberra might one day apologise to the "stolen generations" -- thousands of Aborigines taken from their families by the authorities.

But John Anderson, acting head of the National Party, the junior member of the ruling Liberal-National coalition, said the time was not right for an apology over an official policy that continued into the 1970s and was last week condemned by the country's human rights watchdog as genocidal.

"I think the time will come (for an apology), but it isn't yet, when we've had a chance to fully consider all of the ramifications and put forward the most appropriate response," Anderson said in a television interview.

Prime Minister John Howard told an Aboriginal conference on May 26 that he was personally sorry for what had happened to Aboriginals in the past. But he stopped short of an official apology, later citing legal concerns.

The government has so far resisted mounting pressure to pay compensation and apologise over the almost century-long welfare policy of taking children from Aboriginal families under a forced assimilation scheme.
Howard told Parliament last week that Australians could not be held legally responsible for the sins of past generations.

The Human Rights Commission, in a 700-page landmark report on the policy, last week urged an official apology be made and compensation paid to address the suffering of Aborigines and help steer the country towards racial harmony.
Anderson rejected any comparison between the calls for an apology to Aborigines and Australia's call for an apology from Japan for World War Two atrocities.
"There was not the same degree of ill intent by any means that there was by some of the aggressors of World War Two," he said.

"That doesn't in any way diminish the fact that we have to take this seriously, we have to work this through, and the government does need, we do have the responsibility to consider carefully this report."

The government is already preparing for a substantial compensation payout to Aborigines under its controversial solution to end a divisive national land rights row between farmers and native Australians.

Howard's solution, criticised by both sides and senior National politicians, guarantees farmers the right to land they have leased from the government since European settlement more than 200 years ago.
It also guarantees Aborigines access for traditional use, but limits those rights and in some cases exempts land from Aboriginal claims.
Anderson warned that an early election over the land rights issue would be damaging to the nation.
"I think it would be a regrettable thing to happen. I don't think it would be a healthy thing for the nation," he said.
The constitution allows Howard to call an early election if parliament's upper house, the Senate, twice rejects legislation.
The Labour opposition and other minority parties in the Senate, where the government does not have a majority, have expressed concern over Howard's planned land rights solution.
The Howard plan is aimed at resolving a row sparked by a December High Court ruling that Aborigines still had rights to land leased by the government to farmers.
But the court ruling, known as the Wik judgement, created widespread confusion and uncertainty by failing to define those rights.
